lines.text: The last great land on Earth to be settled by people, reached by canoe across the Pacific. This is the story of New Zealand, Aotearoa.
Maori tradition tells of Kupe, the Polynesian navigator who first found these islands.
Around 1300, voyagers from Polynesia settled here and became the Maori, the people of the land.
From early on came the haka, a group dance of chanting and stamping, for welcome, challenge and celebration.
In 1642, the Dutch navigator Abel Tasman sailed past, the first European known to reach New Zealand, though he never came ashore.
More than a century later, in 1769, James Cook mapped the coasts in detail, opening the way for Europeans to follow.
Early in the nineteenth century, missionaries wrote the Maori language down in Latin letters. Today it is an official language of the country.
In 1840, a settlement was founded on an isthmus between two harbours. It would grow into Auckland, the largest city.
That same year, many Maori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi with the British Crown. Its two versions differ, and it is still debated today.
Wellington was founded too, at the windy southern tip of the North Island, and in 1865 became the capital.
From 1845, the colonial government and Maori fought a long series of wars over land.
Kate Sheppard, born in 1847, would lead the campaign to give the women of New Zealand the vote.
Ernest Rutherford, a farm boy from Nelson, would go on to find the nucleus of the atom and win a Nobel Prize.
In 1886, Mount Tarawera erupted and destroyed the famous Pink and White Terraces.
In 1893, Sheppard's campaign won: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote.
In 1903, the All Blacks played their first test. Their black kit and their haka would become famous wherever rugby is played.
In 1907, the colony became a dominion, a step on the way to full nationhood.
Edmund Hillary, a beekeeper from Auckland, would stand with Tenzing Norgay on top of Everest in 1953, then spend his life helping the Sherpas.
Christopher Luxon, born in 1970, would become prime minister in 2023.
Before him, Jacinda Ardern would lead the country from 2017, through some of its darkest days.
In 1985, French agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour, and the nation was outraged.
Two years later, New Zealand banned nuclear weapons and nuclear-powered ships, choosing its own path in the world.
In 2001, Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings brought its mountains and valleys to cinemas everywhere.
In 2011, an earthquake struck Christchurch, killing a hundred and eighty-five people.
And in 2019, the same city suffered again when a gunman attacked two mosques, killing fifty-one worshippers.
From Kupe's canoe to a nation of its own, Aotearoa's story runs on across the Pacific.
